lower-0862-s9-indices.description: Use positive, zero and negative indices, including powers with the same base.

sections.title: Count factors in a product
sections.label: Products
sections.intro: Write a small power as repeated multiplication before using the shortcut.

blocks.html: When the bases match, a product joins the factor lists. Add the indices.

blocks.prompt:
\(7^{4} \times 7^{1}\) is written as \(7^n\).

Find \(n\).
blocks.hint: Add indices on the same base.
blocks.solution:
Multiplication joins two strings of equal factors. Add their lengths.

\(4+1=5\).

\(5\)

retry.feedback: The powers are both on the same base. For multiplication, add the indices.

blocks.html: Multiplying the indices counts the wrong number of factors.

blocks.prompt:
\(2^{4} \times 2^{1}\) is written as \(2^n\).

Find \(n\).
blocks.hint: Add indices on the same base.
blocks.solution:
Multiplication joins two strings of equal factors. Add their lengths.

\(4+1=5\).

\(5\)

retry.feedback: The powers are both on the same base. For multiplication, add the indices.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Cancel factors in a quotient
sections.label: Quotients
sections.intro: Look for equal factors above and below the fraction bar.

blocks.html: Subtract the denominator's index from the numerator's index. A negative result leaves factors underneath.

blocks.prompt:
Divide \(2^{6}\) by \(2^{7}\).

Write the result as \(2^n\). Find \(n\).
blocks.hint: Subtract the denominator's index.
blocks.solution:
\(6-(7)=-1\). There are more base factors in the denominator.

\(-1\)

retry.feedback: Take the top index minus the bottom index in that order.

blocks.html: Swapping the order of subtraction reverses the fraction.

blocks.prompt:
Divide \(3^{6}\) by \(3^{7}\).

Write the result as \(3^n\). Find \(n\).
blocks.hint: Subtract the denominator's index.
blocks.solution:
\(6-(7)=-1\). There are more base factors in the denominator.

\(-1\)

retry.feedback: Take the top index minus the bottom index in that order.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Read zero and negative indices
sections.label: Reciprocal
sections.intro: Compare the pattern of powers as each step divides by the same base.

blocks.html: For non-zero \(a\), \(a^0=1\) and \(a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^n}\).

blocks.hint: Reverse numerator and denominator.
blocks.solution:
A negative index means take the reciprocal of the positive power.

\(\frac{1}{3}\)

retry.feedback: A negative index changes where the factor sits. It does not make the answer negative.

blocks.html: A negative index does not make a positive base negative.

blocks.hint: Reverse numerator and denominator.
blocks.solution:
A negative index means take the reciprocal of the positive power.

\(\frac{1}{4}\)

retry.feedback: A negative index changes where the factor sits. It does not make the answer negative.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

lower-0862-s9-standard-form.description: Scale numbers by powers of ten and describe very large or very small numbers in standard form.

sections.title: Move across place values
sections.label: Place value
sections.intro: Use the value of each place, rather than imagining a loose decimal point.

blocks.html: Every place to the left is ten times the previous place. Scaling by ten repeatedly follows the index.

figure.alt: Place value rows showing 3.48 and the same digits two columns left as 348
figure.caption: Multiplying by 100 makes each digit count 100 times its former value.

blocks.prompt:
The measurement display starts at \(0.174\).

Find the new reading after multiplying by \(10^4\).
blocks.hint: Count the place-value jumps.
blocks.solution:
Multiplying by \(10^4\) makes every place worth 10,000 times as much.

\(1740\)

retry.feedback: Multiplication by a positive power of ten makes a positive number larger.

blocks.html: Going in the wrong direction makes a number smaller when it should get bigger.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Count the place-value jumps.

sections.title: Read a standard-form number
sections.label: Standard form
sections.intro: Point to the single non-zero digit before the decimal point.

blocks.html: Standard form is \(A imes10^n\) with \(1\leq A<10\) and integer \(n\).

blocks.prompt:
A microscope display gives the number \(0.0000045\). In standard form it is \(A\times10^n\).

Find \(n\).
blocks.hint: Write a coefficient from 1 up to but excluding 10.
blocks.solution:
The coefficient is \(\frac{9}{2}\). The original number is \(10^{-6}\) times as large as this coefficient.

\(-6\)

retry.feedback: Use a negative power for a positive number smaller than 1.

blocks.html: A coefficient of 12.3 must be changed along with its power of ten.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Write a coefficient from 1 up to but excluding 10.
blocks.solution:

\(6\)

retry.feedback: Use a negative power for a positive number smaller than 1.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Scale by a small power of ten
sections.label: Negative exponents
sections.intro: Write a negative power of ten as a fraction when the direction is hard to see.

blocks.html: Dividing by one hundredth multiplies by 100. Check whether your result should grow or shrink.

blocks.prompt:
A counter reads \(1.36\).

Evaluate \(1.36\div10^{-7}\).
blocks.hint: Change division by a reciprocal into multiplication.
blocks.solution:
\(10^{-7}=1/10^7\). Dividing by that fraction multiplies by its reciprocal.

\(13600000\)

retry.feedback: Dividing by a small positive number increases the reading.

blocks.html: Dividing by a number less than 1 can make a positive value larger.

lower-0862-s9-number-types.description: Distinguish rational and irrational numbers and estimate square and cube roots.

sections.title: Classify numbers
sections.label: Rational
sections.intro: Try to write the number as one integer divided by another non-zero integer.

blocks.html: A terminating or recurring decimal is rational. A square root of a positive non-square integer is irrational.

blocks.prompt:
Compare \(\sqrt{125}\), \(\sqrt{121}\), \(\frac{11}{4}\) and \(0.11\).

Which one is irrational?
blocks.hint: Check which square root lies between consecutive integers.
blocks.solution:
125 is not a perfect square. Its square root cannot be written as a ratio of integers.

\(sqrt{125}\)

retry.feedback: Take the root of a perfect square before classifying it.

blocks.html: A radical written with a root sign can still be rational if it simplifies to an integer.

blocks.prompt:

Which one is irrational?
blocks.hint: Check which square root lies between consecutive integers.

\(sqrt{148}\)

retry.feedback: Take the root of a perfect square before classifying it.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Find neighbouring square roots
sections.label: Square root
sections.intro: Place a number between two consecutive perfect squares.

blocks.html: The square root lies between their positive roots. Compare squares before using a calculator.

blocks.prompt:
A square tile has area 87 square units.

Give the whole number just below its side length.
blocks.hint: Compare nearby square numbers.
blocks.solution:
\(81<87<100\). Take the square root of all three numbers.

\(9\)

retry.feedback: The larger integer is the upper bound. You need the whole number just below.

blocks.html: The side length of a square is the square root of its area.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Compare nearby square numbers.

retry.feedback: The larger integer is the upper bound. You need the whole number just below.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.label: Cube root

blocks.html: Compare the volume to nearby perfect cubes. Their edges give lower and upper estimates.

examples.question:
Compare \(\sqrt{38}\), \(\sqrt{36}\), \(3\) and \(0.06\).

  1. Which one is irrational? Options: A. \(sqrt{36}\). B. \(3\). C. \(0.06\). D. \(sqrt{38}\).

lower-0862-s9-expressions.description: Translate verbal rules, apply the order of operations and simplify products and fractions.

sections.title: Read operations in order
sections.label: Order
sections.intro: Use substitution to see which object each operation acts on.

blocks.html: Evaluate brackets, then indices, then products or divisions, then sums or differences.

blocks.prompt:
For a lamp circuit, the value of \(x\) is 9.

Evaluate \(3+2x^2\).
blocks.hint: Apply powers before multiplication and addition.
blocks.solution:
Square 9 first to get 81.

Multiply by 2, then add 3.

\(165\)

retry.feedback: Only the term with an x is multiplied by the square.

blocks.html: Without brackets, an index on x applies to x and not to a coefficient beside it.

blocks.prompt:
For a lamp circuit, the value of \(x\) is 2.

Evaluate \(3+2x^2\).
blocks.hint: Apply powers before multiplication and addition.
blocks.solution:
Square 2 first to get 4.

Multiply by 2, then add 3.

\(11\)

retry.feedback: Only the term with an x is multiplied by the square.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Build an area from four pieces
sections.label: Expand
sections.intro: Split each side of a rectangle into two lengths and pair the pieces.

blocks.html: A product of two brackets has four products before collecting like terms.

figure.alt: An area model split into x squared, three x, two x and six
figure.caption: Each part of the first side pairs with each part of the second side. This sketch is not drawn to scale.

blocks.prompt:
A rectangle has sides \(x+6\) and \(x+5\) units.

Expand the expression for its area.
blocks.hint: Multiply each term in one bracket by both terms in the other.
blocks.solution:
The four pieces are \(x^2+5x+6x+30\).

Add the two terms in x.

\(x^2+11x+30\)

retry.feedback: Show all four products, including the two strips with one x.

blocks.html: Multiplying only the first and last terms misses two strips.

blocks.prompt:
A rectangle has sides \(x+7\) and \(x+5\) units.

Expand the expression for its area.
blocks.hint: Multiply each term in one bracket by both terms in the other.
blocks.solution:
The four pieces are \(x^2+5x+7x+35\).

Add the two terms in x.

\(x^2+12x+35\)

retry.feedback: Show all four products, including the two strips with one x.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Cancel factors in algebraic fractions
sections.label: Fractions
sections.intro: Rewrite each term as a product of simple factors.

blocks.html: Common non-zero factors may be cancelled. Keep any restriction from the original denominator.

blocks.prompt:
Take a non-zero value of \(x\). Consider \(\frac{6x^{5}}{2x^3}\).

Simplify the fraction.
blocks.hint: Divide coefficients and subtract the indices.
blocks.solution:

revision.body:
Read operations in order

Evaluate brackets, then indices, then products or divisions, then sums or differences.

Build an area from four pieces

A product of two brackets has four products before collecting like terms.

Cancel factors in algebraic fractions

Common non-zero factors may be cancelled. Keep any restriction from the original denominator.

Turn words into a rule

Translate one operation at a time. A square, a cube and a root each describe a different rule.

lower-0862-s9-formulae.description: Change the subject of linear, squared and cubed formulae by undoing operations in order and checking which answer fits the context.

sections.title: Undo a multiplier
sections.label: Divide
sections.intro: An area formula can give the area when you know the sides. Changing the subject lets you use the same relationship in reverse. Start by circling the letter you want on its own and reading the right-hand side as a chain of operations.

blocks.html: A subject is a single variable on one side, with coefficient 1. For \(T=kn\) with \(k\ne0\), divide both sides by \(k\): \(n=\frac{T}{k}\). In \(T=kn+c\), undo the addition first, then divide.

figure.alt: An input leads right to an output by multiplying by three, and left by dividing by three
figure.caption: The inverse route retraces the multiplication by dividing by the same non-zero number.

blocks.prompt:
The rule is \(T=kn\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=7\) and \(T=28\).

Find the value of \(n\).
blocks.hint: The operation on \(n\) is multiplication by 7. Divide 28 by 7.

retry.feedback: \(28\) is the output. Divide by 7 to find the input \(n\).

blocks.html: If you divide \(T=kn+c\) by \(k\) first, both terms on the right have to be divided. Subtracting \(c\) first avoids that extra bookkeeping.

blocks.prompt:
The rule is \(T=kn\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=8\) and \(T=32\).

Find the value of \(n\).
blocks.hint: The operation on \(n\) is multiplication by 8. Divide 32 by 8.

retry.feedback: \(32\) is the output. Divide by 8 to find the input \(n\).

blocks.html: If a question asks you to change the subject, keep the other letters. Substitute any supplied numbers afterwards.

sections.title: Undo a square
sections.label: Square
sections.intro: A square hides the sign of a number: squaring 5 or −5 gives 25. A formula may give a condition, such as a physical length being positive, that tells you which root belongs to the problem.

blocks.html: For \(A=ks^2\) with \(k>0\), divide to get \(s^2=\frac{A}{k}\). If \(s\) is a positive length, take \(s=\sqrt{\frac{A}{k}}\). Without a positive-length condition, a positive square can give two signed solutions.

blocks.prompt:
The rule is \(A=ks^2\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=2\) and \(A=72\).

Find the value of \(s\).
blocks.hint: Start by dividing 72 by 2 to isolate \(s^2\). Then identify the positive number that squares to that result.
blocks.solution: \(s^2=\frac{72}{2}=36\). The positive root is \(s=\sqrt{36}=6\).

retry.feedback: \(72\) is the area variable \(A\). First divide by 2, then take the positive square root.

blocks.html: Take the square root of the whole quotient after dividing. In general \(\sqrt{\frac{A}{k}}\ne\frac{\sqrt A}{k}\).

blocks.prompt:
The rule is \(A=ks^2\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=3\) and \(A=108\).

Find the value of \(s\).
blocks.hint: Start by dividing 108 by 3 to isolate \(s^2\). Then identify the positive number that squares to that result.
blocks.solution: \(s^2=\frac{108}{3}=36\). The positive root is \(s=\sqrt{36}=6\).

retry.feedback: \(108\) is the area variable \(A\). First divide by 3, then take the positive square root.

blocks.prompt: The outside side length of a square border is \(s+2\) cm. The total area inside the outside edge is \(81\,\text{cm}^2\). Find \(s\), in centimetres.
blocks.hint: Write \((s+2)^2=81\). What operation undoes squaring the whole bracket?
blocks.solution: The outside side length is \(\sqrt{81}=9\,\text{cm}\), so \(s=9-2=7\,\text{cm}\).

retry.feedback: Nine is the outside side length \(s+2\). Subtract 2 to find \(s\).
The 2 is inside the squared bracket. Take the positive square root before subtracting it.

blocks.html: Check the sign against the context and substitute back into the original formula.

sections.title: Undo a cube
sections.label: Cube
sections.intro: A cube keeps the sign of its input. One real number cubes to any given real result. The cube root is the operation that reverses cubing, so a square-root button will not undo a cube.

blocks.html: For \(V=kr^3\), divide by non-zero \(k\) before taking the cube root: \(r=\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{k}}\). If a bracket is cubed, take the cube root before undoing operations inside that bracket.

blocks.prompt:
The rule is \(V=kr^3\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=6\) and \(V=2058\).

Find the value of \(r\).
blocks.hint: Divide 2058 by 6 to isolate \(r^3\). Then identify a number whose cube equals that result.

retry.feedback: \(2058\) is the volume variable \(V\). First divide by 6, then take the cube root.

blocks.html: The factor \(k\) is outside the cube. Dividing by it isolates \(r^3\), so \(\sqrt[3]{V}\div k\) normally gives a different result.

blocks.prompt:
The rule is \(V=kr^3\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=7\) and \(V=2401\).

Find the value of \(r\).
blocks.hint: Divide 2401 by 7 to isolate \(r^3\). Then identify a number whose cube equals that result.

retry.feedback: \(2401\) is the volume variable \(V\). First divide by 7, then take the cube root.

blocks.html: Before using a calculator, look for a familiar cube, such as \(4^3=64\) or \(5^3=125\).

examples.title: Reverse a formula
examples.question:
The rule is \(T=kn\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=5\) and \(T=10\).

  1. Find the value of \(n\).

    [2]

  2. Make \(n\) the subject of the original formula.

    [2]
solution: (a) Divide by \(k\) to get \(2\).
No further operation is needed.
(b) First divide both sides by the multiplier.
No further operation is needed.

examples.title: Find the side from a fencing formula
examples.question: A rectangular enclosure has length \(L\), width \(w\) and perimeter \(P=2L+2w\). Make \(w\) the subject. Then find the width when \(P=30\,\text{m}\) and \(L=9\,\text{m}\).
solution: The term with \(w\) is \(2w\). Subtract \(2L\) from both sides: \(P-2L=2w\).
Divide the whole left side by 2: \(w=\frac{P-2L}{2}\).
Substitute the measurements: \(w=\frac{30-18}{2}=6\,\text{m}\).
Check that two lengths and two widths give \(18+12=30\,\text{m}\).

examples.title: Reverse a formula
examples.question:
The rule is \(A=ks^2\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=9\) and \(A=81\).

  1. Find the value of \(s\).

    [2]

  2. Make \(s\) the subject of the original formula.

    [2]
solution: (a) Divide by \(k\) to get \(9\).
Take the positive square root of both sides.
(b) First divide both sides by the multiplier.
Take the positive square root of both sides.
\(s=\sqrt{\frac{A}{k}}\)

examples.title: Read the length from the area of two squares
examples.question: Two identical square mats with side \(s\) cover \(A=98\,\text{cm}^2\) in total. Make \(s\) the subject of \(A=2s^2\), then find \(s\).
solution: One mat has half the total area: \(s^2=\frac{A}{2}\).
A side length is positive, so \(s=\sqrt{\frac{A}{2}}\).
With \(A=98\), one square has area \(49\,\text{cm}^2\), so the side is \(7\,\text{cm}\).

examples.title: Reverse a formula
examples.question:
The rule is \(V=kr^3\). The variables are positive. For this case, \(k=4\) and \(V=500\).

  1. Find the value of \(r\).

    [2]

  2. Make \(r\) the subject of the original formula.

    [2]
solution: (a) Divide by \(k\) to get \(125\).
Take the cube root of both sides.
(b) First divide both sides by the multiplier.
Take the cube root of both sides.

examples.title: Undo a cube and then a shift
examples.question: A cube has edge length \(t+1\) centimetres. Its volume is \(V=(t+1)^3\). Find a formula for \(t\), then find \(t\) when \(V=125\).
solution: The whole bracket is cubed. Take the cube root first: \(t+1=\sqrt[3]{V}\).
Subtract 1 from both sides to get \(t=\sqrt[3]{V}-1\).
For \(V=125\), \(t=5-1=4\). The edge length is \(5\,\text{cm}\), so the volume is \(125\,\text{cm}^3\).

glossary.definition: The variable that appears alone on one side.
An operation that reverses another.
A number or expression multiplying a variable.
The real number that gives the original value when cubed.

revision.body:
Read the operations in reverse

In \(T=kn+c\), subtract \(c\), then divide by \(k\): \(n=\frac{T-c}{k}\).

Isolate the power

For \(A=ks^2\) with a positive length, \(s=\sqrt{\frac{A}{k}}\). For \(V=kr^3\), \(r=\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{k}}\). In each formula \(k\ne 0\).

Check by going forwards

Put your new expression into the original formula. The operations should undo one another.
revision.checks:
A cube has edge length \(t+2\) cm and volume \(216\,\text{cm}^3\). Find \(t\).

Check. \(t+2=\sqrt[3]{216}=6\), so \(t=4\).

lower-0862-s9-equations-limits.description: Translate a situation into an equation or inequality and interpret the bounds of a rounded result.

sections.title: Represent a cost
sections.label: Charge
sections.intro: Decide which part is paid once and which part depends on the quantity.

blocks.html: A fixed charge is a constant. A repeated charge is a coefficient times the number of repeats.

blocks.prompt:
An art club charges 2 tokens once, then 7 tokens per session. The bill is 37 tokens.

Find how many sessions were booked.
blocks.hint: Separate the fixed charge from the charge per session.
blocks.solution:
\(7n+2=37\).

Subtract 2 from both sides and divide by 7.

\(5\)

retry.feedback: Remove the fixed charge before dividing.

blocks.html: The full bill includes both charges, so dividing the whole amount by the rate can overcount.

blocks.prompt:
An art club charges 2 tokens once, then 8 tokens per session. The bill is 42 tokens.

Find how many sessions were booked.
blocks.hint: Separate the fixed charge from the charge per session.
blocks.solution:
\(8n+2=42\).

Subtract 2 from both sides and divide by 8.

\(5\)

retry.feedback: Remove the fixed charge before dividing.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Solve with an unknown denominator
sections.label: Denominator
sections.intro: List the input that would cause division by zero before solving.

blocks.html: Multiply both sides by the denominator, then solve the resulting equation. Check the original restriction.

blocks.prompt:
Consider the equation \(\frac{14}{x+2}=2\) for real x.

Find \(x\).
blocks.hint: Undo division first, then isolate x.
blocks.solution:
Multiply both sides by the non-zero denominator to get \(14=2(x+2)\).

Divide by 2, then subtract 2.

\(5\)

retry.feedback: The quotient gives x plus the added constant. Subtract that constant.

blocks.html: An answer that makes the original denominator zero is never a solution.

blocks.prompt:
Consider the equation \(\frac{21}{x+2}=3\) for real x.

Find \(x\).
blocks.hint: Undo division first, then isolate x.
blocks.solution:
Multiply both sides by the non-zero denominator to get \(21=3(x+2)\).

Divide by 3, then subtract 2.

\(5\)

retry.feedback: The quotient gives x plus the added constant. Subtract that constant.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Write an inequality
sections.label: At most
sections.intro: Decide whether the number at the limit is permitted.

blocks.html: At most means less than or equal to. Divide by a positive coefficient without reversing the sign.

blocks.prompt:
A device starts at 50 degrees. Its temperature falls by 6 degrees each minute. It works only while the temperature is at least 2 degrees.

For how many whole minutes can the device keep working?
blocks.hint: Translate ‘at least’ before isolating t.
blocks.solution:
\(50-6t\geq 2\).

After subtracting 50, divide by -6. Reverse the inequality sign.

\(8\)

retry.feedback: At the limit the temperature is exactly the minimum, so this minute is allowed.

blocks.html: If you divide by a negative coefficient, the direction of the inequality changes.

blocks.prompt:
A machine uses 2 units to start and 7 units per hour. It can use at most 58 units in total.

Find the longest whole number of hours it can run.
blocks.hint: Translate ‘at most’ into less than or equal to.
blocks.solution:
\(7x+2\leq 58\).

Subtract 2 and divide by 7. Equality is allowed.

\(8\)

retry.feedback: At most includes the case where the full allowance is used.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

sections.title: Find the possible original values
sections.label: Rounding
sections.intro: Locate the midpoints between consecutive rounded values.

blocks.html: The lower limit is half a step below the recorded value. The upper limit is half a step above.

figure.alt: A number line has a filled point at 45 and an open point at 55, with 50 in the middle
figure.caption: For positive values rounded to 50 to the nearest 10, include 45 and exclude 55.

blocks.prompt:
The recorded reading is 1,740, rounded to the nearest 10 units.

Give the lower limit.
blocks.hint: Subtract half of the rounding step.

retry.feedback: The full step is too large. Move only halfway to the previous rounded value.

blocks.html: For positive values rounded in the usual way, the upper endpoint rounds to the next recorded value.

blocks.prompt:
The recorded reading is 1,180, rounded to the nearest 10 units.

Give the lower limit.
blocks.hint: Subtract half of the rounding step.

retry.feedback: The full step is too large. Move only halfway to the previous rounded value.

blocks.html: Show the step that explains your answer.

A device starts at 26 degrees. Its temperature falls by 4 degrees each minute. It works only while the temperature is at least 2 degrees.

  1. For how many whole minutes can the device keep working?

    [2]

  2. Write the original comparison and solve it for t.

    [2]
solution: (a) \(26-4t\geq 2\).
After subtracting 26, divide by -4. Reverse the inequality sign.
(b) When dividing by a negative number, the direction changes.

Subtract 2 and divide by 5. Equality is allowed.
(b) The coefficient of x is positive, so the inequality sign stays the same.

revision.body:
Represent a cost

A fixed charge is a constant. A repeated charge is a coefficient times the number of repeats.

Solve with an unknown denominator

Multiply both sides by the denominator, then solve the resulting equation. Check the original restriction.

Write an inequality

At most means less than or equal to. Divide by a positive coefficient without reversing the sign.

Find the possible original values

The lower limit is half a step below the recorded value. The upper limit is half a step above.

Check. \(5\)

lower-0862-s9-linear-systems.description: Solve simultaneous linear equations by elimination or intersection. Create and check two equations for a count-and-value problem.

sections.title: Remove one variable
sections.label: Eliminate
sections.intro: One equation can allow many pairs. A simultaneous solution is the pair that satisfies both. Write the equations in the same order so that the coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\) line up.

blocks.html: Elimination makes one variable vanish. Equal terms such as \(+2y\) and \(+2y\) disappear when you subtract; opposite terms such as \(+2y\) and \(-2y\) disappear when you add. You can multiply a whole equation first to create a matching pair.

blocks.prompt:
Solve \(2x+y=10\) and \(3x+y=13\) together.

Give the solution as an ordered pair (x, y).
blocks.hint: Both equations have \(+y\). Subtract the equation with \(2x\) from the one with \(3x\), so the totals become \(13-10\).
blocks.solution:
Subtract the first equation from the second to get \(x=13-10=3\).

Use the first equation for \(y=10-2(3)=4\). The solution is \((3,4)\).

retry.feedback: Your first coordinate fits. Use \(y=10-2x\) to find the second coordinate, then check both equations.

blocks.html: If you multiply an equation by 2, multiply every term on both sides, including the total. Subtract a whole equation in brackets so you handle its signs correctly.

blocks.prompt:
Solve \(2x+y=12\) and \(3x+y=16\) together.

Give the solution as an ordered pair (x, y).
blocks.hint: Both equations have \(+y\). Subtract the equation with \(2x\) from the one with \(3x\), so the totals become \(16-12\).
blocks.solution:
Subtract the first equation from the second to get \(x=16-12=4\).

Use the first equation for \(y=12-2(4)=4\). The solution is \((4,4)\).

retry.feedback: Your first coordinate fits. Use \(y=12-2x\) to find the second coordinate, then check both equations.

blocks.html: Combining the equations gives one variable. Substitute it back to find the other, then check the pair in both originals.

sections.title: Find where lines meet
sections.label: Intersect
sections.intro: Every point on a line fits its equation. A point at the crossing has the same horizontal and vertical coordinates on both lines. Start with the graph for an estimate; use the equations if a coordinate falls between grid lines.

blocks.html: When both equations already give \(y\), set the two expressions for \(y\) equal. After solving for \(x\), use either equation to find \(y\). If the lines have the same gradient but different intercepts, there is no crossing.

figure.alt: The lines y equals x plus 1 and y equals 7 minus x cross at (3, 4).
figure.caption: The marked crossing fits both equations: \(3+1=4\) and \(7-3=4\).

blocks.prompt:
Two lines have equations \(y=6x-24\) and \(y=-x+11\).

Give the intersection as an ordered pair (x, y).
blocks.hint: At the crossing the two \(y\)-values agree, so start with \(6x-24=-x+11\).
blocks.solution:
At an intersection \(6x-24=-x+11\), so \(x=5\).

Substituting in either line gives \(y=6\). Both rules give the intersection \((5,6)\).

retry.feedback: Your first coordinate fits. Use \(y=-x+11\) to calculate the matching second coordinate.

blocks.html: The \(y\)-intercepts show where the separate lines meet the vertical axis. An intersection between the lines must lie on both at the same time.

blocks.prompt:
Two lines have equations \(y=7x-36\) and \(y=-x+12\).

Give the intersection as an ordered pair (x, y).
blocks.hint: At the crossing the two \(y\)-values agree, so start with \(7x-36=-x+12\).
blocks.solution:
At an intersection \(7x-36=-x+12\), so \(x=6\).

Substituting in either line gives \(y=6\). Both rules give the intersection \((6,6)\).

retry.feedback: Your first coordinate fits. Use \(y=-x+12\) to calculate the matching second coordinate.

blocks.prompt: The lines are \(y=2x+1\) and \(y=2x+4\). Which statement about them is correct?
blocks.hint: Compare the gradients and the two \(y\)-intercepts.
blocks.solution: Both gradients are 2, but the \(y\)-intercepts are 1 and 4. The lines are distinct and parallel.

retry.feedback: \((0,1)\) lies on the first line only. At \(x=0\) the second line has \(y=4\).
Two lines with equal gradients are the same line only if their intercepts also agree.
\((0,4)\) lies on the second line only. At \(x=0\) the first line has \(y=1\).

blocks.html: Write the coordinates in the order \((x,y)\). If you read them from a graph, check the scale on each axis.

sections.title: Make two conditions
sections.label: Modelling
sections.intro: Start a word problem by giving each unknown a clear meaning and unit. A count condition tells you how many items there are. A value condition weighs each type by its price, points or similar contribution.

blocks.html: Use the same letters in both equations. In a count-and-value problem, multiply the count equation by one unit value; subtract it from the value equation to isolate the extra contribution from the other type.

blocks.prompt:
At a plant sale, 14 plants are sold. A herb costs 2 credits and a flower costs 3 credits. The total is 35 credits.

Give an ordered pair (herbs, flowers).
blocks.hint: If all 14 plants cost 2 credits, the total would be 28. Each flower adds one credit to that total.
blocks.solution:
Let \(h\) be herbs and \(f\) flowers. Then \(h+f=14\) and \(2h+3f=35\).

Subtract twice the count equation: \(f=35-28=7\). Then \(h=14-7=7\), so the answer is \((7,7)\).

retry.feedback: Keep the plant count at 14. With this many herbs, choose the number of flowers that makes both the count and the value fit.

blocks.html: A count must make sense as a whole number. Check both totals with the roles attached to the variables; a reversed pair can still pass the count check.

blocks.prompt:
At a plant sale, 15 plants are sold. A herb costs 2 credits and a flower costs 3 credits. The total is 37 credits.

Give an ordered pair (herbs, flowers).
blocks.hint: If all 15 plants cost 2 credits, the total would be 30. Each flower adds one credit to that total.
blocks.solution:
Let \(h\) be herbs and \(f\) flowers. Then \(h+f=15\) and \(2h+3f=37\).

Subtract twice the count equation: \(f=37-30=7\). Then \(h=15-7=8\), so the answer is \((8,7)\).

retry.feedback: Keep the plant count at 15. With this many herbs, choose the number of flowers that makes both the count and the value fit.

blocks.html: Put your answer back into the story, naming which number goes with each item.

examples.title: Match both conditions
examples.question:
Solve \(2x+y=12\) and \(3x+y=17\) together.

  1. Give the solution as an ordered pair (x, y).

    [2]

  2. Check your ordered pair in both conditions.

    [1]
solution: (a) Subtract the first equation from the second. The y terms cancel.
Put this value back into either equation.
(b) Substitute the two values together and check both totals.
Both conditions are true.

examples.title: Scale one equation and add
examples.question: Solve \(2x+y=8\) and \(3x-2y=5\).
solution: The \(y\)-coefficients have opposite signs. Double the first equation to get \(4x+2y=16\).
Add to the second equation: \(7x=21\), so \(x=3\).
Using the first equation, \(y=8-2(3)=2\). The pair is \((3,2)\).
Check the second equation: \(3(3)-2(2)=5\).

examples.title: Match both conditions
examples.question:
Two lines have equations \(y=2x-11\) and \(y=-x+10\).

  1. Give the intersection as an ordered pair (x, y).

    [2]

  2. Check your ordered pair in both conditions.

    [1]
solution: (a) At an intersection, both equations give the same y-value.
Solving gives x = 7. Then y = 3.
(b) Substitute the two values together and check both totals.
Both conditions are true.

examples.title: Use a graph to estimate and equations to check
examples.question: The lines \(y=x+1\) and \(y=7-x\) are drawn on the same axes. Find their intersection.
solution: The rising and falling lines have different gradients, so there is a single crossing.
At the crossing the two \(y\)-values agree: \(x+1=7-x\). Then \(2x=6\) and \(x=3\).
Both line rules give \(y=4\), so the exact intersection is \((3,4)\).

examples.title: Match both conditions
examples.question:
At a plant sale, 14 plants are sold. A herb costs 2 credits and a flower costs 3 credits. The total is 33 credits.

  1. Give an ordered pair (herbs, flowers).

    [2]

  2. Check your ordered pair in both conditions.

    [1]
solution: (a) If x is herbs and y is flowers then \(x+y=14\) and \(2x+3y=33\).
Double the first equation and subtract it from the second. That gives y.
Put y = 5 into the first equation to find x.
(b) Substitute the two values together and check both totals.
Both conditions are true.

examples.title: Check whether the totals are possible
examples.question: A team claims to have hit a target 12 times for a total of 35 points. Each hit scores either 2 points or 5 points. Can both totals be correct?
solution: Let \(a\) be the number of 2-point hits and \(b\) the number of 5-point hits. Then \(a+b=12\) and \(2a+5b=35\).
If every hit scored 2 points, the total would be \(24\). Each 5-point hit contributes 3 extra, so subtracting the doubled count equation would give \(3b=35-24=11\).
This would make \(b=\frac{11}{3}\), which cannot count hits. The two totals cannot both be true for these scoring rules.

revision.body:
Eliminate a variable

Match coefficients by multiplying an entire equation if needed. Subtract equal signed terms; add opposite signed terms. Substitute to get the second coordinate.

Find an intersection

At a crossing, both line rules give the same \(y\) for the same \(x\). Equal gradients with different intercepts give parallel lines.

Model and check

Define each unknown. For a count-and-value problem, build one equation for the count and one for the total value.

sections.title: Connect radius, diameter and perimeter
sections.label: Radius
sections.intro: Measure from the centre to the edge. Double this length to go all the way across.

blocks.html: \(C=\pi d=2\pi r\) is a distance around the boundary and \(A=\pi r^2\) describes the area inside.

figure.alt: A circle with a diameter through its centre and the right half marked radius

blocks.prompt:
A model track is a circle. Its diameter is 52 m.

The circumference is kπ metres. Find k.
blocks.hint: Multiply the diameter by π.
blocks.solution:
Use \(C=\pi d\). The diameter is already given.

\(52\pi\text{ m}\)

retry.feedback: The measurement is already a diameter. Do not double it again.

sections.title: Join areas along a common edge
sections.label: Add

blocks.html: Write a separate area for each piece. A semicircle contributes half the area of a complete circle.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: A semicircle is half a circle.

Halve \(144\pi\) to get the semicircle.

\(72\pi\text{ m}^2\)

retry.feedback: The curved piece is only half a full circle.

lower-0862-s9-compound-percentages.description: Use multipliers for repeated increases and decreases. Compare the final amount with the original to find the overall percentage change.

sections.title: Use a multiplier for growth
sections.label: Growth
sections.intro: A percentage increase uses the current amount as its whole. After one increase that whole is larger. For a second increase at the same rate, the number of points or credits added is larger as well.

blocks.html: Keep the original \(100\%\) and add the increase. A \(20\%\) rise gives \(120\%=1.20\). Use one factor for each round, so two rounds with the same increase give \(\text{starting amount}\times1.20^2\).

figure.alt: A starting bar of 100 percent and an increased bar of 120 percent
figure.caption: An increase of 20% means multiply the current amount by 1.20.

blocks.prompt:
A club account begins at 450 credits. It gains 15% each round for two rounds.

Find the final total.

Give a monetary amount in credits to two decimal places if you round.
blocks.hint: Start with 450 credits and use multiplier \(1.15\). Use that factor again on the result for round 2.
blocks.solution: For two rounds the balance is \(450\times 1.15^2=595.125\) credits. This is 595.13 credits to two decimal places.

retry.feedback: The first gain leaves \(517.5\) credits. Apply the second \(15\%\) increase to that amount.

blocks.html: Two \(20\%\) increases do not give \(40\%\) overall. The second increase is based on the result of the first.

blocks.prompt:
A club account begins at 500 credits. It gains 15% each round for two rounds.

Find the final total.
blocks.hint: Start with 500 credits and use multiplier \(1.15\). Use that factor again on the result for round 2.
blocks.solution:
The first multiplier is 1.15. It gives 575.

Multiply this amount by 1.15 to get 661.25.

\(\frac{2645}{4}\)

retry.feedback: The first gain leaves \(575\) credits. Apply the second \(15\%\) increase to that amount.

blocks.html: Write the multiplier before putting the numbers into a calculator. Keep full precision until you give the requested final value.

sections.title: Use the percentage left
sections.label: Decrease
sections.intro: A loss removes only part of the current amount. The part left after the first loss becomes the whole for the next round. A multiplier between zero and one makes a positive amount smaller.

blocks.html: For a \(15\%\) decrease, keep \(85\%=0.85\). To find what is left after two equal decreases, multiply by \(0.85\) twice. To find how much was lost, subtract the final value from the original.

blocks.prompt:
A club account begins at 250 credits. It loses 25% each round for two rounds.

Find the final total.
blocks.hint: A loss of \(25\%\) leaves \(75\%\). Multiply the 250 credits by \(0.75\) once for each loss.
blocks.solution:
The first multiplier is 0.75. It gives 187.5.

Multiply this amount by 0.75 to get 140.625.

\(\frac{1125}{8}\)

retry.feedback: After the first loss, \(187.5\) credits remain. Find \(25\%\) of that new amount for the second loss.

blocks.html: Multiplying by \(0.15\) finds the first amount lost. Multiplying by \(0.85\) finds the first amount that remains.

blocks.prompt:
A club account begins at 300 credits. It loses 25% each round for two rounds.

Find the final total.
blocks.hint: A loss of \(25\%\) leaves \(75\%\). Multiply the 300 credits by \(0.75\) once for each loss.
blocks.solution:

\(\frac{675}{4}\)

retry.feedback: After the first loss, \(225\) credits remain. Find \(25\%\) of that new amount for the second loss.

blocks.html: Check the direction. A decrease must produce a result below the amount it was applied to.

sections.title: Compare the final value with the start
sections.label: Mixed
sections.intro: To describe the overall change, compare the final amount with the amount before any changes. With two percentages, work out what stays or grows at each step, then combine those factors.

blocks.html: The overall multiplier is the product of the individual multipliers. A product of \(1.08\) is an overall increase of \(8\%\); a product of \(0.92\) leaves \(92\%\), an overall decrease of \(8\%\).

blocks.prompt:
An event had 900 points. Its total grows by 30%, then falls by 15% of the new amount.

Find the final total.
blocks.hint: Multiply the 900 points by \(1.30\) to increase them. Multiply your result by \(0.85\) to keep the required amount.
blocks.solution:
The first multiplier is 1.3. It gives 1170.

Multiply this amount by 0.85 to get 994.5.

\(\frac{1989}{2}\)

retry.feedback: The starting value for the fall is \(1170\) points after the increase. Keep \(85\%\) of that value.

blocks.html: A rise and an equal percentage fall use different amounts as their reference values. Multipliers such as \(1.20\) and \(0.80\) do not multiply to 1.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Multiply the 950 points by \(1.30\) to increase them. Multiply your result by \(0.85\) to keep the required amount.
blocks.solution:

\(\frac{4199}{4}\)

retry.feedback: The starting value for the fall is \(1235\) points after the increase. Keep \(85\%\) of that value.

blocks.prompt: A tank reading first rises by \(25\%\) and then falls by \(20\%\) of its new value. What is the overall percentage change? Enter 0 if there is no change.
blocks.hint: Compare \(1.25\times0.80\) with 1.
blocks.solution: The total multiplier is \(1.25\times0.80=1\), so there is no overall percentage change.

retry.feedback: Subtracting the percentages uses the same starting amount for both. Find the product of the two multipliers.
The final reading is \(100\%\) of the start. The question asks for the percentage change.
The percentages refer to different starting values. Find the combined multiplier before deciding the overall change.

blocks.html: Give the percentage and say whether it is an increase or decrease when the question asks for an overall change.

examples.title: Use the new amount for the second percentage
examples.question:
A club account begins at 300 credits. It gains 5% each round for two rounds.

  1. Find the final total.

    [2]

  2. Give the total percentage change. State whether it is an increase or a decrease.

    [2]
solution: (a) The first multiplier is 1.05. It gives 315.
Multiply this amount by 1.05 to get 330.75.
(b) Divide the final amount by the start. Subtract 1 to get the signed change, then multiply by 100.
10.25% increase.

examples.title: Compare a repeated rise with one larger rise
examples.question: A club has 200 points. Plan A adds \(10\%\) each round for two rounds. Plan B adds \(20\%\) once. Which plan finishes with more points?
solution: Plan A gives \(200\times1.10=220\) in the first round. A tenth of 220 is 22, so the second round gives 242.
Plan B adds \(20\%\) of the original 200, so it gives \(200\times1.20=240\). Plan A also grows the extra 20 points awarded in its first round.
Plan A finishes 2 points ahead; the two-round multiplier is \(1.10^2=1.21\).

examples.title: Find how much was used over two days
examples.question: A container holds 160 litres of water. Each day, the garden uses \(25\%\) of the water still in the container. How much is left after two days and how much has been used in total?
solution: Each day keeps \(100\%-25\%=75\%\), so the daily multiplier is \(0.75\).
After one day, \(160\times0.75=120\) litres remain. After two days, \(120\times0.75=90\) litres remain.
The amount used is \(160-90=70\) litres. The daily amounts used are 40 litres and 30 litres.

examples.title: Use the new amount for the second percentage
examples.question:

    [2]
solution: (a) The first multiplier is 1.2. It gives 900.
Multiply this amount by 0.85 to get 765.
(b) Divide the final amount by the start. Subtract 1 to get the signed change, then multiply by 100.
2% increase.

examples.title: Decide whether opposite changes cancel
examples.question: A score of 250 increases by \(20\%\), then decreases by \(20\%\). State the final score and the overall percentage change.
solution: After the increase the score is \(250\times1.20=300\). The decrease removes a fifth of 300, which is 60.
The final score is 240. In one calculation, the combined multiplier is \(1.20\times0.80=0.96\).
The score ends at \(96\%\) of its original value, a decrease of \(4\%\).

related.title: Order of operations with fractions and decimals

glossary.definition: A single factor used to scale an amount.
Several changes where every step starts with the preceding result.
The amount immediately before the next percentage change.
The difference between final and original amounts, expressed relative to the original.

revision.body:
Choose the multiplier

Increase by \(p\%\): multiply by \(1+\frac{p}{100}\). Decrease by \(p\%\): multiply by \(1-\frac{p}{100}\).

Apply every change

Multiply the factors. For two \(10\%\) falls the combined multiplier is \(0.90^2=0.81\), so \(81\%\) is left and \(19\%\) was lost.

Compare with the original

A product above 1 means a rise. A product below 1 means a fall.
revision.checks:

revision.examTip: Leave rounding until you have applied all the multipliers.

lower-0862-s9-ratio-models.description: Share in a ratio and decide whether a fixed unit rate or a fixed product applies.

sections.title: Build a bar of equal parts
sections.label: Shares
sections.intro: Use one bar which contains all the parts stated in the ratio.

blocks.html: For a ratio of 2 to 3, there are five equal parts. Divide the total by five to find one part.

figure.alt: Two blue equal parts and three yellow equal parts forming one five-part bar

blocks.hint: Add the parts before finding the value of one part.
blocks.solution:
There are 18 equal parts. Each part contains 3 counters.

Use 13 parts for red.

\(39\)

sections.title: Look for a fixed price per unit

blocks.html: In direct proportion, multiplying one quantity by a factor multiplies the other by the same factor.

Multiply this by 3.

sections.title: Look for a fixed product

sections.intro: Think about a fixed job shared among equal workers.

blocks.html: In inverse proportion, multiplying one quantity by a factor divides the other by the same factor.

lower-0862-s9-sequencing.description: Generate terms, identify equal or growing differences and describe nth term rules.

sections.title: Match a common difference
sections.label: Linear
sections.intro: Compare the difference between every two neighbouring terms.

blocks.html: In a linear sequence, the common difference is the multiplier of n. Use an early term to find the constant.

blocks.prompt:
Here are the first terms of a linear sequence: \(\frac{9}{2}\), \(6\), \(\frac{15}{2}\), \(9\).

Give the value of term 5.
blocks.hint: Find the common difference, then match the first term.
blocks.solution:
The common difference is \(\frac{3}{2}\).

The rule is \(\frac{3}{2}n+3\) because position 1 gives \(\frac{9}{2}\).

\(\frac{21}{2}\)

retry.feedback: You have the multiplier. Also match the first term to find the constant.

blocks.html: The first term corresponds to n = 1, not n = 0.

blocks.prompt:
Here are the first terms of a linear sequence: \(-1\), \(-5\), \(-9\), \(-13\).

Give the value of term 5.
blocks.hint: Find the common difference, then match the first term.
blocks.solution:
The common difference is \(-4\).

The rule is \(-4n+3\) because position 1 gives \(-1\).

\(-17\)

retry.feedback: You have the multiplier. Also match the first term to find the constant.

Use \(n^2-5\).

\(20\)

lower-0862-s9-compound-rates.description: Read speed and density as gradients. Convert units, use changes along a segment and compare two rates on a common scale.

sections.title: Choose the correct units
sections.label: Speed
sections.intro: A rate tells you how much of one quantity corresponds to one unit of another. In metres per second, a speed of 3 means that at a steady speed you travel 3 metres in each second.

blocks.html: For a straight distance–time segment, \(\text{speed}=\frac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{elapsed time}}\). Pick two points on the segment and subtract their coordinates. A line through the origin lets you use zero as one point.

figure.alt: A rising straight line with its y-intercept and a right-angled rise and run marked
figure.caption: The gradient is rise divided by run. The intercept is the value at x = 0.

blocks.prompt:
A cycle route's distance–time graph is a straight line through the origin. After 10 minutes it reaches 120 metres.

Find the speed in metres per minute.
blocks.hint: Use \(120\) metres as the change in distance and \(10\) minutes as the elapsed time.
blocks.solution: The line starts at zero, so the speed is \(\frac{120}{10}=12\,\text{m/min}\).

retry.feedback: Your division is in the opposite order. Metres per minute means \(120\div10\).

blocks.html: A reading at time 5 is not necessarily the distance covered since the start of the given segment. Subtract the two distance readings and the two times.

blocks.prompt:
A cycle route's distance–time graph is a straight line through the origin. After 10 minutes it reaches 130 metres.

Find the speed in metres per minute.
blocks.hint: Use \(130\) metres as the change in distance and \(10\) minutes as the elapsed time.
blocks.solution: The line starts at zero, so the speed is \(\frac{130}{10}=13\,\text{m/min}\).

retry.feedback: Your division is in the opposite order. Metres per minute means \(130\div10\).

blocks.prompt: A runner covers \(900\,\text{m}\) in \(3\,\text{min}\) at a steady speed. Find the speed in metres per second.
blocks.hint: The numerator is already in metres. Convert the three minutes to seconds before dividing.
blocks.solution: \(3\,\text{min}=180\,\text{s}\), so the speed is \(900\div180=5\,\text{m/s}\).

retry.feedback: \(300\) is the number of metres per minute. Divide it by 60 or use \(180\,\text{s}\) for the journey time.
That is the time per metre. For metres per second, divide distance by elapsed time.

blocks.html: Choose the time unit first. Use \(1\,\text{min}=60\,\text{s}\) when the question asks for metres per second.

sections.title: Compare slopes with a common scale
sections.label: Compare speeds
sections.intro: Two cyclists can cover different distances and still have the same speed if they travel for different times. Compare rates in the same units or compare how far each goes in one equal time interval.

blocks.html: On the same distance–time axes, the higher speed gives the steeper straight line. If each graph uses its own scale, calculate both gradients before comparing.

blocks.prompt:
Two straight distance–time lines start at zero. Route A covers 44 m in 4 seconds. Route B covers 46 m in 4 seconds.

By how many metres per second is route B faster?
blocks.hint: Find the rates \(44\div4\) and \(46\div4\) in metres per second. How much larger is the second rate?
blocks.solution: Subtract the speeds: \(\frac{46}{4}-\frac{44}{4}=\frac{2}{4}=0.5\,\text{m/s}\).

retry.feedback: Two metres is the distance difference after 4 seconds. Divide the distance difference by 4 to find the speed difference.

blocks.html: A point drawn higher on the page can indicate a later time or a different scale. It does not by itself identify the faster cyclist.

blocks.prompt:

sections.title: Compare masses for equal volumes
sections.label: Density
sections.intro: Density compares the mass of equal amounts of space. Imagine two solid cubes of identical size. The heavier cube has the greater density because it packs more mass into the same volume.

blocks.html: With volume on the horizontal axis and mass on the vertical axis, the gradient of a straight line through the origin is \(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\). On common axes the steeper line belongs to the denser material.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.solution: \(\text{density}=\frac{7}{7}=1\,\text{g}/\text{cm}^3\).

blocks.html: With mass in grams and volume in cubic centimetres, the result is in grams per cubic centimetre. Swapping the numerator and denominator changes both the number and its unit.

blocks.html: To recover volume, divide mass by density. Check that the grams cancel and the result is in cubic centimetres.

Time (min)Distance (m)
2180

solution: The distance increases by \(720-180=540\,\text{m}\). The time elapsed is \(5-2=3\,\text{min}\).

The second skater is \(6-5=1\,\text{m/s}\) faster, even though the second recorded distance is smaller.

examples.title: Use density to choose the less bulky block
examples.question:
Two samples
MaterialVolume (cm³)Mass (g)
P824
Q630

A model-maker needs a \(60\,\text{g}\) block. Which material takes up less space, and what volume does it take?
solution: Material P has density \(24\div8=3\,\text{g}/\text{cm}^3\). Material Q has density \(30\div6=5\,\text{g}/\text{cm}^3\).
Q is denser, so a block of the same mass needs less space. The volumes are \(60\div3=20\,\text{cm}^3\) for P and \(60\div5=12\,\text{cm}^3\) for Q.
Choose Q. Its block takes up \(12\,\text{cm}^3\).

revision.body:
Send a point along its ray

With a positive scale factor, each image point stays on the same ray from the centre through its original point.

Recover the centre and factor

Extend two distinct vertex-to-image lines to find their intersection. The ratio of image distance to original distance gives the factor.

Scale two lengths to find an area

Each new length is k times its old length. So area is k² times the old area.

Scale a one-dimensional measure

Every side changes by the same factor. Add them after scaling, or multiply the old perimeter by that factor.

revision.body:
Separate two yes-or-no attributes

A Venn diagram shows the overlap directly. A Carroll diagram uses a row and a column for the two answers.

Read tallies and tables

Check row and column totals. A frequency is a count and is different from the data value being counted.

Compare sets of bars

Dual bars place groups next to each other. Compound bars stack groups, which makes totals easy to see.

Turn a fraction into a sector

A category's share of 360° is its frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°.

lower-0862-s9-chart-choices.description: Choose and interpret time series, frequency polygons, scatter graphs and back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagrams.

sections.title: Connect successive readings in time
sections.label: Time
sections.intro: Choose a time series when the order and timing of repeated readings matter. A classroom temperature record can show when the room warmed up and when it cooled. Start by reading the two axes and their units.

blocks.html: Put time on the horizontal axis and the measurement on the vertical axis. Space the times on a consistent scale and join successive points. A join helps you see the trend between readings; intermediate values are estimates.

figure.alt: Readings at 0, 5 and 15 minutes are 12, 18 and 24 degrees Celsius. The first segment is steeper.
figure.caption: The horizontal gap from 5 to 15 minutes is twice the gap from 0 to 5 minutes.

MinuteTemperature in °C

Give the rise in temperature between the first two readings, in degrees Celsius.
blocks.hint: Read the temperatures at minutes 14 and 19. Subtract the earlier reading from the later reading.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the first reading, 6°, from 11°.

\(5\)

retry.feedback: \(11^\circ\text{C}\) is the later reading. Subtract \(6^\circ\text{C}\) to find the rise.

blocks.html: Equal gaps between dots on the page must represent equal time intervals. If two observations are further apart in time, show a larger horizontal gap.

blocks.html: To decide which interval changed faster, compare change per unit of time. Looking at the two changes alone works only when the intervals are equally long.

sections.title: Plot grouped data at the midpoints
sections.label: Polygon
sections.intro: A grouped table tells how many values fall in an interval. A frequency polygon helps compare the sizes of those groups by drawing one point for each class.

blocks.html: Add the two ends of a class and divide by 2 to get its midpoint. Plot the midpoint on the horizontal axis and its frequency on the vertical axis. Join adjacent points in order from left to right.

figure.alt: The frequency polygon has points (15, 4), (25, 9) and (35, 6).
figure.caption: Each plotted point uses a class midpoint and the frequency for that class.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: The middle interval starts at 40 and ends at 50. Take the average of those ends.
blocks.solution:
The middle group runs from 40 up to 50. Its midpoint is 45.

\(45\)

retry.feedback: 40 is the lower end of the middle interval. A frequency polygon places the point halfway across the class.

blocks.html: A point at \(x=25\) and frequency 9 can represent nine values in the whole class centred at 25. It does not tell you that nine observations were exactly 25.

blocks.html: If the question asks for a modal class, give the interval for the highest point, rather than just its midpoint.

sections.title: Keep paired data together
sections.label: Scatter
sections.intro: Use a scatter graph to look for a relationship between two quantities measured for the same people, objects or places. Pair the measurements before plotting; every dot represents one object with both measurements.

blocks.html: A general rise from left to right suggests positive association; a general fall suggests negative association. Look at the spread as well as the direction. A point that sits far from the pattern may be an outlier.

figure.alt: Four points rise with walking distance while the point at 3 kilometres and 18 minutes sits below the pattern.
figure.caption: Positive association can still be visible when one point is far from the trend.

sections.title: Order scores around a shared stem

blocks.html: Put the shared stems in the centre of a back-to-back diagram. Put one group on the left and the other on the right. Within a row, read each group outwards from the centre to see its leaves in ascending order.

revision.body:
Choose a chart to match the data
QuestionDisplayWhat to plot
How does a reading change over time?Time seriesTime and reading
How many values are in each class?Frequency polygonMidpoint and frequency
Are paired quantities associated?Scatter graphOne dot per pair
Which group has the higher median?Back-to-back stem-and-leafOrdered leaves on shared stems

State what the chart can show

A point on a frequency polygon describes a whole class, and a scatter graph shows association. A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps the original individual values.

lower-0862-s9-compare-and-question.description: Compare averages and spread, recognise misleading graphics and improve a statistical study.

sections.title: Choose a centre and a spread
sections.label: Summaries
sections.intro: Read a sorted set before finding its middle or its repeated value.

blocks.html: Mean uses every value, median gives the middle, and mode gives the most frequent. Range is largest minus smallest.

blocks.prompt:
Group A records 18, 22, 22, 25, 27. A second group has median 23 and range 11.

blocks.hint: Find the spread from maximum minus minimum.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the smallest result, 18, from the largest result, 27.

\(9\)

blocks.html: One summary measure may hide differences seen in another measure.

sections.title: Use results to plan the next investigation

sections.intro: Decide which claim your data support and where its limits are.

blocks.html: Ask a statistical question, collect suitable data, analyse it and reconsider both your conclusion and your method.

figure.alt: Four steps connected in a loop: ask, collect, analyse, review
figure.caption: Look back at the question and decide what to change or investigate next.

Choose a centre and a spread

Mean uses every value, median gives the middle, and mode gives the most frequent. Range is largest minus smallest.

Use a midpoint for each group

Inspect an infographic's scale

A cut-off bar scale can make a small change look much bigger. A picture's size can also suggest a misleading comparison.

Use results to plan the next investigation

Ask a statistical question, collect suitable data, analyse it and reconsider both your conclusion and your method.
